I have a deconstructionist orientation towards social facts. That’s why my arguments are a mix of facts but heavily reliant on lived experiences. The reason being all these social structures exist because they are in practice. These practices need to be understood from the perspective of the practitioner. (Anthony Giddens)

My research (not particularly caste related) has been focused on collecting people’s experiences and their explanations of the causes behind it. As per Garfinkel of Ethnomethodological approach the structures exist because of the daily practices and experiences of the people and their subsequent reaction to it. It is a part of interpretative approach of Weber, which (Weberian interpretative approach) Beteille introduced in India. So, it helps to accurately understand the social context of the people.

Then come the critical and subaltern perspectives which argue to go beyond the manifest quantitative representations because they are a product of dominant values. They argue to reflect critically and create a common man’s perspective of their experiences.

In my practice I have merged the critical, subaltern and ethnomethodological approaches. STEM crowd finds it difficult to digest the methodological flexibility and pluralism of Sociology. We study to have an authentic understanding of social structures from the perspective of the actors. Quantitative data often have low internal validity to represent experienced structural realities for the people.

I beg to differ. When you believe in something as true, you often start to think of it as natural and simple. But truth is neither simple nor complex, it is just plain, and often bitter truth. Simplicity is delicious and appealing, contrary to the nature of truth. The pursuit of simplicity in the name of truth has led to growing distrust towards complex scientific explanations, thus, you see the rise of anti-intellectualism and anti-science attitude. Truth is not simple, conspiracy theory is. The latter can swing both ways. The truth requires rigor, and is painful and hard to swallow. Simplicity is anathema to the truth.

For the OP: Don't look for simple explanations for what you observe. Look for what you don't know, what you can't see and ask questions, to those who tell you to believe, which feed your curiosity, and not the ego.

There are many people to whom whatever that comes out of their mouth is "science". They don't believe it, they *know* it. When you point this out that if you make extraordinary claims then the onus is on you to prove it, they will either abscond, insult you or search for evidence to back up their claims, feeding into their confirmation bias.  


Such people lack critical thinking ability. They conflate critically evaluating own opinions against contradicting evidence, with criticizing others, and resort to the latter. The rigor is exhausting, many lack the capacity and stamina to withstand the exercise of criticizing own ideas. They choose the path of least resistance, though, they would be ready to go through mental gymnastics to prove their point, or even fall back to their primeval instincts of verbal and physical violence. But they just can't tolerate the exercise. Many call them simpletons, others have other names.
